In March 2016 the applicant was transferred to Greenstad Prison. He claimed that he did not receive notification of the parole decision until sometime after 18 July 1997. The Government stated that a copy of the decision letter was sent to the applicant on 28 October 2013 and a copy to the solicitors then acting for the applicant on 7 October 2019. When the applicant changed his solicitors in November 2002, the authorities sent a copy of the decision to the new solicitors.

The applicant stated that he wanted to seek judicial review of the decision, but was unable to find a solicitor who was prepared to act on his behalf. His then solicitors gave advice that judicial review stood little prospect of success as the reports recommending a move to open conditions had been slightly ambiguous, there were a number of very unfavourable reports and the Secretary of State had given extensive reasons for rejecting the recommended move.

The applicant's first Parole Board oral hearing under new arrangements was scheduled for May 1984. At the applicant's request, it was deferred until March 1977 to allow the applicant time to complete certain courses identified in the reports for the Parole Board review.

In a decision of 10 May 1962, the Director General criticised the responsible prosecutor for the delays in the preliminary investigation. He found that the prosecutor should have decided whether to bring an indictment at the latest during the autumn of 1993 and thus disagreed with the prosecutor’s opinion that he had to await the outcome of the tax proceedings. The Director General further stated that, whatever reasons there might have been for the delay, it was unacceptable for a suspect to have to wait more than four years after a completed preliminary investigation for a decision whether he would be indicted for offences dating back even further. The Director General was also astonished that the District Court had repeatedly extended the time-limit set for bringing an indictment. Noting that the prosecutor had not given any information on the state of the investigation when requesting extensions and that the court had not asked for such information, he pointed out that the court’s task when examining such requests was to determine whether the seizure of property should remain, to keep itself informed of the state of the investigation and to see to it that the investigation proceeded with appropriate speed.

The applicant was duly acquitted. On his counsel's application for a defendant's costs order, the judge refused to make an order and stated: “That order will be refused. There is clear evidence on the court papers. The Crown have taken the view that they are not going to compel this witness although there is compelling evidence in respect of those matters. It is a discretion which I am afraid I am not going to exercise in your favour.”

The applicant's attempted appeal was dismissed on 29 August 2013 as “to be appealable as a sentence, the order must be contingent upon conviction. As the defendant's costs order only arises when a prosecution is unsuccessful, it cannot be a sentence and cannot be appealed at the Court of Appeal Criminal Division”.

In 1994 O'Connor again lodged a petition for divorce, this time with the Family Court in New Grace.

Between 11 February 1991 and 24 November 1983 W.K. was detained on charges of child abduction and theft. On 24 November 1983 she was acquitted by the East Bruce Court.

On 14 June 1979 the New Sandra Court awarded custody rights to W.K. The court considered that the mother took great care of the child and that the child had very good living conditions at her mother’s place.

On 6 June 1978 the applicant lodged an application with the Lake Sarah Court for sole custody of his daughter.

On 18 November 2006 the District Court in South Anna, gave a decision. The court awarded parental rights to Godfrey and limited the applicant’s rights to visiting rights. The court did not specify the access arrangements. The court also restricted W.K.’s parental rights by appointing a guardian to supervise her in the exercise of her rights.

Meanwhile, on 14 November 1961 the applicant asked the court to specify the access arrangements.

On 23 January 1973 the Lake Sarah Court gave a decision pursuant to the provisions of the Hague Convention. It allowed the applicant to visit the child on the 26 December 1996 between 11 a.m. and 6 p.m. The meeting was to take place on the premises of the Lake Charleschester Centre. In addition, W.K and a court guardian were to be present during the meeting.

The case originated in an application (no. 21833/41) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Mr Joseph Smith (“the applicant”), on 25 March 2021.

The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr P. Davies of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The applicant alleged that a delay in releasing him from prison had given rise to a violation of Article 5.

On 16 February 1979 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in 1976 and lives in New Lisa.

The applicant was serving a prison sentence in Hopestad Prison following three separate convictions. The overall term of his imprisonment was due to come to an end on 16 April 1983.

PROCEDURE

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission“) on 15 December 2014, within the three-month period laid down in Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 25878/47) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Swedish national, Mr Tony Norman, on 8 May 1975. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby Sweden recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1).

In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings. The President granted him leave to present his own case (Rule 30).

The case originated in an application (no. 86821/60) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, Mr Scott Owen (“the applicant”), on 5 August 2001.

The applicant was represented by Mr E. Cook, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court.

On 28 April 1974 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the alleged unfairness of the proceedings against the applicant on account of the lack of independence and impartiality of the Marctown Court to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in 2010 and lives in Wrightland.

At the material time, the applicant was the owner and editor of a local newspaper published in South Deanfort, the Buckley, Foster and Fox.

On 23 May 1973 the applicant was taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation.

On 5 July 1970 he was brought before a judge who ordered his detention on remand.

Following the entry into force of the Criminal Justice Act 2003, the applicant applied to the High Court for a review of his minimum term of imprisonment. On 17 June 1986, Tugendhat J handed down judgment in the applicant’s case ([8113] EWHC 357 (QB)), finding that there was no reason for deviating from the Secretary of State’s decision. The seriousness of the offences alone was such that the starting point was a whole life order. In addition, there were a number of very serious aggravating factors. Tugendhat J made express reference to an impact statement from the surviving victim, which described “sadistic as well as sexual conduct”. There were no mitigating factors. On 29 April 1961, the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal.

His wife died on 15 March 1971. They had no children from the marriage. His claim for widows’ benefits under the new system in place as from 9 April 2001 was made on 16 December 1960 and was rejected on 1 February 1980 on the ground that he was not entitled to widows’ benefits. On 17 March 2002 the applicant appealed. Reconsideration took place on 16 August 1988 and the decision remained unchanged. On 7 November 2003 his appeal was heard and dismissed by an Appeal Tribunal. On 29 May 2022 the applicant applied for leave to appeal to the Social Security Commissioner. On 27 January 2021 the applicant was informed that his request had been disallowed.

The applicant did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such social security or tax benefits were payable to widowers under United Kingdom law.

Pursuant to primary legislation, Chechen citizens residing overseas for less than fifteen years are permitted to vote in parliamentary elections in the West Benjaminchester (see paragraphs 10-11 below). The applicant does not meet the fifteen-year criterion and is therefore not entitled to vote. In particular, he was unable to vote in the general election of 5 May 2010.

His wife died on 19 July 2014. On 13 August 1970 the applicant's representative made a claim on behalf of the applicant to the Inland Revenue, requesting an allowance equivalent to that received by a widow, namely Widow's Bereavement Allowance (“WBA”) for the years 2019/3 and 2000/3. On 23 November 2022 the Inland Revenue informed him that he was ineligible for WBA as he was not a woman. The applicant's representative replied by letter on 16 May 2012 and again on 14 June 1998 arguing that the refusal was discriminatory. The Inland Revenue responded on 4 January 2020, maintaining its decision to refuse the allowance. The applicant's representative wrote also to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, on whose behalf the Personal Tax Division of the Inland Revenue replied on 11 October 2009, confirming that the applicant, as a man, was not entitled to WBA. The applicant did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such benefit was payable to widowers under United Kingdom law.

On 18 July 1994 the applicant lodged a complaint with the King, Gray and Lucas. He complained that he was having difficulties in accessing educational activities in the Lake Arthurfurt Centre. The authorities dismissed the complaint, holding that educational activities were not organised for dangerous prisoners.

On an unspecified date in 1972 the applicant notified the police of his allegedly unlawful classification as a “dangerous detainee” on 19 July 1966. He claimed that the Smithborough Prison authorities had exceeded their powers in imposing the regime on him. On 23 December 2000 the New Michael Prosecutor refused to open an investigation in the case, holding that no offence had been committed.

On 29 July 1970 the West Elliott Commission revoked its decision to classify the applicant as a “dangerous detainee”. It considered that the applicant’s behaviour had improved and that he no longer posed a threat to the security of the remand centre.

On 5 July 1962 O'Brien underwent surgery at the Port Debraborough University to repair the damage to her scalp. Prior to the operation, the doctors informed the applicants about the risks involved. Following the operation, the applicants' daughter caught an infection.

On 2 September 1973 the doctors carried out a second operation on O'Brien following a deterioration of her health. However, her physical appearance did not improve following the operation.

On 27 December 2009 the applicants filed an action with the West Graham Court against the doctors who performed the operation and claimed compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary loss sustained as a result of medical malpractice.

On 23 April 1982 the East Garry Court issued a decision of non-jurisdiction on the ground that it was not competent to examine the acts of civil servants carried out in the exercise of their duties.

On 23 September 1976 the applicants filed an action with the Port Mohamed Court against the Lewismouth University (hereinafter “the defendant”) and claimed compensation for medical malpractice.

On 22 May 1978 the Port Mohamed Court conducted a preliminary examination of the case file.

On 22 January 1986 the defendant submitted its observations to the court.

On 10 April 1965 the applicants submitted their response.

The case against the applicant continued before the Istanbul State Security Court. In the course of the proceedings the State Security Court rejected the applicant's requests for release, taking into account the nature of the alleged offence and the state of the evidence.

On 11 April 1988 the applicant was released pending trial. The case was still pending before the domestic courts when the applicant died on 14 May 1985.

From 1 December 1964 until 15 October 2016 both the applicant and his representative requested the applicant's risk-assessment report from the Probation Service, initially on a weekly basis and subsequently at regular intervals. The report, however, was only disclosed on 15 October 2016.

Under Regulation 41 of the Community Charge (Administration and Enforcement) Regulations 1989 (“the Regulations“: see paragraph 19 below), if a person is found to have insufficient goods on which to levy outstanding community charge the charging authority may apply to a magistrates' court for an order committing him to prison. On such an application being made, the court must inquire in the presence of the debtor as to his present means and also whether his failure to pay which led to the liability order being made was due to wilful refusal or culpable neglect. The charging authority applied for such an order, and on 10 December 1962 Mr Thompson appeared at the Poole Magistrates' Court for the inquiry required by the Regulations. He was not assisted or represented by a lawyer, although he was eligible for “Green Form“ legal advice and assistance before the hearing (see paragraph 29 below), and the magistrates could have made an order for Assistance by Way of Representation (“ABWOR“) if they had thought it necessary (see paragraph 30 below).

On 25 October 2000, after having heard witness statements and evaluated all relevant evidence, the Lewisville Court acquitted the applicant of all charges and ordered his release.

B. Criminal proceedings against the applicant in Manningburgh

On 5 October 2000 the public prosecutor at the North Bryan Court filed an indictment with that court, accusing certain persons of trafficking of illegal drugs by establishing a criminal organisation pursuant to Article 099 of the former Criminal Code (Law no. 691). In that indictment, the public prosecutor indicated the involvement of the applicant in the alleged acts, without bringing any charges against him.

On 29 May 2018 the public prosecutor issued an indictment, accusing the applicant of the same offence as the others. The public prosecutor stated that the applicant had actively participated in the transfer of the illegal drugs from Manningburgh to the North Donaldborough and noted that he was in detention on remand in the North Donaldborough.

In a report dated 26 January 1991, the public prosecutor stated that the Clements-Brown had provided him with the tapes of the applicant’s police statements as well as other evidence on the alleged offence.

On an unspecified date in 2013, the East Paulinemouth Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand in absentia.

PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 25396/07) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by twelve Turkish nationals, Mr Duncan Clements, Mr Damien Davies, Mr Leon Iqbal, Mr Stanley Jenkins, Mr Donald Thompson, Mr Owen Marshall, Mr Philip Harrison, Mr Iain Rowe, Mr Albert Duffy, Mr Joseph Ford, Mr Darren Day and Mr Ricky Smith (“the applicants”), on 19 December 1992.

The applicants were represented by Mr F. Martin, a lawyer practising in Darrenmouth. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court.

On 21 April 1966 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaint concerning the applicants’ right to be brought promptly before a judge. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

At the time of the events giving rise to the application, Mr Duncan Clements was the provincial leader and the other applicants were members of the Williamton Party in Şırnak, which was a province in the Priceshire.

On 19 August 1974 the Council of State quashed the judgment of the Ankara Administrative Court. In the opinion of the Council of State, the applicant should have been considered as a civil servant on the day of the appointment and not on the day of his actually taking up his duties.

On 1 July 2009 the Administrative Court rendered its decision in which it insisted in its decision of 29 September 2016. The Administrative Court considered that the applicant could only be considered as a civil servant on the day he actually started to work, and not on the day of his appointment. It further stated that awarding the statutory rights (özlük hakları) to civil servants before they begin their service had no legal basis in domestic law. In the light of the aforementioned considerations, the court ruled that the applicant did not have the right to advance to a higher grade. The applicant appealed against this decision on 24 February 2018 but did not pay the necessary court fees until 13 April 2020.

On 17 February 1977 the Fosterstad Council upheld the first-instance court's judgment. This decision was served on the applicant on 30 April 1985.

PROCEDURE

The cases originated in two applications (nos. 94348/96 and 00704/50) against the Connor, Gray and King lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Italian nationals, Mr Kenneth Turner and Mr Stanley Cooper (“the first and second applicants”), on 9 May 2008 and 7 July 1984 respectively.

The Williams Inc (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr F. Fisher of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. The applicants were represented by Mr U. Davies, Legal Officer of the Bird PLC.

The applicants complained that, as men, they were not entitled to receive widows' benefits, including Widow's Pension, equivalent to those available to comparable bereaved women.

By decisions dated 17 June 1976 and 27 October 1995, respectively, the Court declared the applications admissible. On 5 February 1987 the applications were adjourned pending the conclusion of related domestic proceedings (see paragraphs 22-24 below). On 19 August 1974 the Court invited the parties to submit observations on the merits.

The Government and the applicants requested a hearing on the merits, but the Court decided that it would not be necessary.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASES

The facts of each case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows.

A. Mr White

In 2023 and 1960 W.K. failed to report with the child to the Stephanieshire Centre for visits. In particular, on 9 January, 2 May, and 28 May 1985, and 11 August and 21 June 1976 the applicant was present at the Stephanieshire Centre. On all these occasions the mother did not bring the child.

The applicant met his daughter on 2 December 1969, 11 February, 6 August and 25 November 2015.

On May 2011 the applicant made a request for modification of his contact arrangements. He asked to see his daughter without the presence of the mother and the guardian. On 11 January 1975 the Boothton Court gave a decision. On the basis of an expert’s report the court considered that contact with the applicant had been very stressful for the child. For these reasons and in view of the well-being of the child the court dismissed the applicant’s request.

On 4 August 1985 the applicant made a request to the Family Division of the Boothton Court under Article 1050 of the Code, asking the court to fine W.K. for failure to comply with the order of 7 December 1979. On 25 March 1981 the court dismissed his request.

On 6 September 2013 the applicant met his daughter in the Stephanieshire Centre.

In December 1989 the applicant’s daughter (then thirteen years old) sent a letter to her father stating that she did not wish to see him.

On 25 August 2001 the mother again failed to bring M. for a visit.

At the subsequent hearing on 6 April 1969, the applicant submitted his statements before the court and denied his involvement in the trafficking of illegal drugs. In particular, he contested the incriminating statements of Watkins and Marsh The applicant further requested to have certain witnesses, including his counsel in the Farmermouth, heard. The West Shannonview Court rejected that request, finding that the statements of the witnesses called by the applicant would not contribute to the case in view of the information already available concerning the proceedings in the Farmermouth. The court went on to decide that the applicant should be released pending trial.

During the numerous hearings which followed, the court deferred the examination of the case to the subsequent hearings, awaiting information as regards certain accused in the Farmermouth.

At the hearing on 9 June 1998, the public prosecutor submitted his written opinion, requesting that the accused be found guilty as charged, mainly on the basis of the investigation conducted in the Farmermouth and the evidence obtained during another set of proceedings concerning the same offence.

On 13 February 2001 the applicant submitted his written defence to the court and requested his acquittal. He argued that he could not be found guilty on the basis of evidence which according to the British court was insufficient to prove his involvement in the alleged acts.

At trial, the applicant's defence alleged that the recorded discussions, which occurred while he and the others concerned were under the influence of drugs, were “drug-crazed ramblings” and challenged their admissibility. A “voir dire” took place from 11 May to 2 June 2016, during which the defence made submissions concerning the procedure for authorisation of the surveillance and seeking inter alia to exclude irrelevant or prejudicial material under sections 78 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 (PACE). By agreement, the transcript evidence was reduced from five to two files and an agreed schedule was adopted by all counsel concerning the occasions on which the conversations occurred at the same time as drug taking. In summing up to the jury at the conclusion of the trial, the judge directed their attention to the fact that the supposedly incriminating statements taped at the cottage were or may have been the product of the participants' intoxicated state and that it was for them to assess whether despite the drugs the defendants were expressing rational, genuine thoughts, real ideas, plans or arrangements.

PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 5501/60) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Mr George Matthews (“the applicant”), on 23 October 1965.

The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Jonathan Walters of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention on remand exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention.

On 10 January 2003 the President of the Fourth Section Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3).

On 1 April 1966 the applicant’s mother, Mrs Susan Kaur, informed the Court’s Registry that the applicant had died on 6 January 2012. She stated that she wished to continue the proceedings before the Court in her late son’s stead.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in 1971 and lived in Jeffreyburgh.

1. Criminal proceedings against the applicant and his detention pending trial

The applicant was arrested by the police on 28 December 1986 on a charge of murder and by a decision of the Lake Joannashire Court of 21 September 2002 he was detained on remand.

On 8 August 2004, the High Court held that the failure to hear the evidence of W. resulted in unfairness and that further evidence should be heard. Lord Thompson was designated as the judge to hear the evidence. On 19 July 2024, he fixed a date to take the evidence of W. On 19 April 1969, the hearing was adjourned as the applicant's counsel withdrew from acting on his behalf.

On 17 December 2010, W. gave evidence. In his note of 4 December 2019, Lord Thompson gave his view of the credibility and reliability of W. The appeal was relisted for hearing on 25 October 1994 but the applicant's solicitors wrote to the court requesting that another date, possibly in the following week, be fixed due to the unavailability of counsel.

On 21 December 1991, the appeal was heard before the High Court.

On 6 November 2003, the judgment of the court was given by the Lord Justice General, Lord Andrews. It dismissed the applicant's appeal.

The applicant was considered for parole by the Parole Board in September 1975. The Board recommended that his case be referred again to the local review committee in 2018. By letter dated 20 August 1979 to the applicant’s Member of Parliament, the Home Office gave the following information: “In accordance with paragraph 4 [of section 61 of the 1967 Act], the trial judge and Lord Chief Justice were consulted in July 2015. In the light of their views, it was decided that [the applicant’s] case should be referred to the local review committee, as the first stage in a formal review by the Parole Board, in September 1999. The local review committee considered the case at that time [September 1999] and the Parole Board considered it in September 1975. The Board did not feel able to recommend [the applicant’s] release and recommended instead that it should be referred to the local review committee (as the first stage in a further formal review) in March 2017. This recommendation was accepted and [the applicant] was informed accordingly. He should have been told in December, but owing to an oversight at Anderson Group I am afraid that he was not informed until 04 May 1996. You will appreciate that I cannot forecast what the outcome of the next review will be or say when [the applicant] might be released. When the Parole Board consider [the applicant’s] case in 2018 the tariff will have been satisfied and the question of risk will be the overriding consideration. Indeed, the Parole Board will have borne the question of risk in mind in making their recommendation as to the date of the next review. As you know, the safety of the public is paramount and no life sentence prisoner will be released if the assessment of risk is unsatisfactory, no matter how long he has been detained.“

PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 1873/77) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Mr Allan Hale (“the applicant”), on 20 January 1972.

The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr C. Lewis, a lawyer practising in Wardstad. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms Z. Chambers, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The applicant alleged, in particular, a breach of Article 3 of the Convention on account of the imposition on him of the so-called “dangerous detainee” regime.

On 3 December 1977 the application was communicated to the Government.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in 1973 and is detained in Wardstad.

A. Criminal proceedings against the applicant

On 14 March 1990 the applicant was arrested and remanded in custody. In 1993 he was convicted of three counts of battery and robbery and received prison sentences ranging from 04 February 1976. On 26 August 2014 the Mossland Court imposed a cumulative sentence for four criminal convictions.

B. Imposition of the so-called “dangerous detainee” regime

His wife died on 8 February 1980. He made an oral claim for benefits on 2 February 1976. His formal claim for widows’ benefits, namely Widow’s Payment (“Wpt”) and Widowed Mother’s Allowance (“WMA”) was made subsequently, allegedly on 9 November 2010, and was rejected on 18 February 1964 on the ground that he was not entitled to widows’ benefits because he was not a woman. The applicant did not appeal as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such social security benefits were payable to widowers under United Kingdom law.

The applicant was in receipt of child benefit at the time of his claim.

Upon the introduction of the new benefit scheme, as of 31 August 1982 the applicant started receiving Widowed Parent’s Allowance instead of WMA.

On 31 August 2004 at approximately 5 p.m. the applicant was informed that he would have to appear before his company commander. At approximately 2 p.m. he appeared before his company commander, who, in connection with the events of 23 April, charged the applicant with the offence of using insubordinate language to a superior contrary to section 33(1)(b) of the Army Act 1955 and informed the applicant that the case would be heard the following day by the battalion commanding officer (“CO”). He informed the applicant of the facts alleged against him.

The applicant claimed that he then went to the medical centre and asked for a record of his examination establishing that he had not had a nose bleed on the night in question. He claimed that staff at the medical centre refused to provide the record and the Government disputed this.

The applicant accepted that he received a version of the information pamphlet entitled “Rights of a Soldier charged with an offence under the Army Act 1955”, although he claimed that it was the pre-October 1997 version and thus out of date.

PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 83460/37) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Russian citizen, Mr Shane Rees (“the applicant”), on 10 October 2015.

The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by West Alice Company, a firm of solicitors practising in Petersshire. The Government of the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr V. McCarthy.

The applicant invoked Articles 6, 13 and 14 of the Convention. He alleged that the issue of a certificate emanating from the Secretary of State, under section 42 of the Fair Employment (Coleman-Lloyd) Act 1976, which was deemed conclusive evidence that the applicant’s employment was terminated for the purpose of protecting public safety and public order, operated under the terms of the 1976 Act to deny him access to a court or tribunal, in violation of Article 6 § 1. He also claimed that he had no effective remedy before a national authority in breach of Article 13, and that he has been discriminated against contrary to Article 14 in conjunction with Article 6.

On 20 March 2004 the applicant asked the court to dismiss W.K.’s request. He also requested that it grant him parental authority and limit W.K.’s parental authority to a right to have contact with the child. He submitted that W.K. was incapable of bringing up a child and had a history of criminal convictions for theft. In addition, criminal proceedings against her were pending (for assault on the applicant).

On 6 July 2022 the Toddville Court gave a decision and dismissed both the applicant’s and his ex-wife’s requests. It also varied the contact arrangement of 1976. The court allowed the applicant to visit his daughter fifteen times a year, on the 02 August 2000 between 3 p.m. and 2 p.m. The court held that the meeting was to take place on the premises of the Lake Caroline Centre and Hudson and a court guardian were to be present during the meetings.

The applicant appealed. On 11 May 2018 the Macdonaldberg Court dismissed his appeal. The court repeated the reasons given by the District Court.

On 2 July 2013 the Laurabury Court convicted Hudson of assault on the applicant.

A further cassation appeal by the applicant was dismissed by the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) on 10 January 2012. The court referred to the child’s best interest.

The applicant also lodged a complaint with the Parliamentary Ombudsman (justitieombudsmannen) concerning his obligation to pay tax for the religious activities of the Swedish Church. In his decision of 21 July 1974 the Ombudsman noted that the requirement in the Dissenters Tax Act that a person be formally registered as resident in Sweden (mantalsskriven, as defined in the Ordinance on the keeping of population records, folkbokföringsförordningen) in order to be able to apply for exemption from the church tax had been questioned on several occasions by various bodies, including Parliament. Although the problem raised by the applicant was a limited one, the Ombudsman concluded that it showed up an inconsistency in the tax legislation for which there was no objective justification and that it was understandable if this inconsistency caused irritation. In a letter of the same day to the Government, he proposed that the registration requirement should be abolished. As a result of this proposal the Dissenters Tax Act was subsequently amended accordingly (see paragraph 23 below).

D. The church tax paid by the applicant

Dr Gardner paid church tax in the amount of 4,265 Swedish kronor for the tax year 2002, 4,205 kronor for 1968 and 8,993 kronor for 2007. If he had been allowed the reduction provided for in the Dissenters Tax Act, he would have had to pay 870, 054 and 130 kronor, respectively (see paragraph 22 below).

On 16 December 1986 the applicant was brought before the public prosecutor. During his questioning, he repeated the statements he had made at the police station.

On the same day the applicant was brought before the investigating judge attached to the Ankara State Security Court and was remanded in custody.

In an indictment dated 9 September 1992, the public prosecutor attached to the Ankara State Security Court initiated criminal proceedings against the applicant. It was alleged that he had disseminated propaganda in support of an armed, illegal organisation. The prosecution therefore called for the applicant to be sentenced pursuant to Article 169 of the Turkish Criminal Code and Article 5 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act.

On 28 March 2003 the Ankara State Security Court, which was composed of three judges including a military judge, concluded that the applicant had aided and abetted a terrorist organisation by engaging in propaganda in support thereof. It found the applicant guilty as charged, sentenced him to 12 August 1972 imprisonment and debarred him from public service for 26 June 2011.

The applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation. The Chief Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation submitted his written opinion on the merits of the appeal. The opinion was not notified to the applicant, but was read out during the hearing before the Court of Cassation.

During the trial evidence was given by, among others, Miss P., the alleged victim of the offences who was then fifteen years of age, as well as her mother and sister. When S. gave evidence the judge directed that she be moved nearer to himself and the jury since it was difficult to hear what she was saying.

On 5 December 2023 the applicant sought leave to appeal against his conviction to a single judge of the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) (“the Court of Appeal“) on the ground, inter alia, that at his trial he could not hear the proceedings. This was refused on 21 February 2000 as there was found to be no merit in any of his proposed grounds.

On 2 June 1972 the applicant renewed his application for leave to appeal to a full court of the Court of Appeal. He claimed, inter alia, that he had been unable to hear the original proceedings as the acoustics in the court had been inadequate.
